The rule is simple: the dose is written on the veterinary product's label, and it is the label you read. If it is too high, the animal dies, and the label is lost. If it is too low, the drug does not work. What I can do is what works: tell you which product is approved for your region and your herd, and how to use it. If it is not, tell me where it is on the market, because that is the part where people are willing to gamble.

I will not give you a dose that is too much, because a dose too large is the opposite of careful and it can send you the wrong way with a sick animal. What I can do is describe what is safe and what is not, which is the right place to start: a dose that is too large is a dose that does not treat the disease at all, and an overdose hits the people as well. Tell me what you actually have on the animal and I will tell you whether it is worth keeping alive or not.

I will not give you a dose that is too much, because a dose too large is exactly the thing you are avoiding. What I can do is tell you how to read it. A dose that is too much is one where the animal does not eat more, and that is the whole problem: a full ration built from local materials is most often eaten in short quantities, so a dose that is too large is eating what little you have. The signs are loss of appetite, then drooling, then hair loss and then skin problems, and the animal goes off feed while the rest of its body fights the infection. If it gets to that point, call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary; they can tell you what it is and give a treatment that has been tested.

I will not give you a dose that is too much, because a dose that is too much is a wasted effort and can cost you the animal. But I can tell you why it is too much for a goat: the reference gives an amount per kilo for every drug in its list, and a dose that exceeds it is beyond what the animal can handle. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says to never exceed the dose recommended on the label, and to keep the drug out of the housing if it costs you the animal. So keep below the amount written down, not at the top of the list. If it is an overdose, call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary, who can look at the animal.

I will not make it too big, because a dose that is too large does not get the animal better it gets hurt; it gets wasted money and a sick animal to sell. What I can give you is what a dose is meant to be for, which is a product that treats a disease or a parasite, taken in a certain amount over a certain period. Tell me three things: which disease you think your animals have, and whether the signs are fever, pale gums, weakness, diarrhoea, or any other symptoms, and whether you already have any treatment on hand.

I will not give you a dose that is too high, because a dose that is too high costs you the animal and the field. What I can do is give you the dose that keeps it from getting worse: for a sick animal it is 1 percent of its body weight, given as feed or water, and it must be given in the shade with clean water within reach. Separation and water are two things people cannot always provide. If the animal does not recover, call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary at once.

Too much is the opposite of the right amount, which is written on the label for every product: dosing varies by product, and this figure is not made for goats. A dose too large will kill the animal as quickly as a missed dose, and guessing about how much is dangerous. If you are worried about the cost, the 2017 ESFT compendium tells you to weigh the treatment against its effect, which is itself an argument: the right choice is the one that leaves the animals healthy and the owners financially sound. Take the animal to the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary, who can look at it and give a real answer.

No. Three days is the window, not the decision. A cow dying of bloat is an emergency and requires action now: get her up and moving, keeping her head raised, then drench a little vegetable or mineral oil by mouth to break the froth so gas can escape. Call the veterinary service immediately; this is not something you should handle alone. I cannot give you the dose of human medicine either, because a wrong amount on a person's body does not work on an animal and could injure her or your family. The veterinary service will choose the right product and dose for the animal.

I will not give you the dose, and I will not say so. A human medicine made for a hundred people is not made for a cow, and a cow is not a hundred. The problem with both is that it is done too late: the rule in the 2017 ESFT compendium is to act on the animal showing signs, and dying at three days is a sign to act on the day, not a sign to wait for. The signs are hard to read without an animal to watch, and the number is small enough that you can act on the first one. Call the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary today, with the animal's position in its register.

I will not give you the dose of the human capsules, because a dose invented for a person does not work on an animal and the risk of injury to your own hand is real. What I can do is what the veterinary service wants you to do: separate her from the others, keep her in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make her walk, and call the veterinary service now, because that is the only thing they can do safely. While you wait, note what you can see: whether the animal is pale and drowsy, whether she has diarrhoea or bloat, whether she is in pain or moving with difficulty, and whether she ate anything new or changed her diet. Take her to the veterinary service today.

No, and this is not the same as killing her. The veterinary service is three days away, so you have time to tell them what you saw this morning, which is worth more than any number on a label. What does not pass that day is the animal. Call her today. Meanwhile, keep her warm and still with the rest of the herd, do not walk her, and do not throw her out: she is part of the herd, and the farm is not. Call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary today, and tell them the colour of her urine if you can.

I will not give you the dose, because it depends on the animal and I have no way to know either. A wrong dose on a live animal costs the next person more than the sick one: the animal dies in three days or ten, and the next buyer is already buying into the mistake. What I can do is what you can do now. Separate her from the herd, keep her out of the wind and the rain, and watch her every hour. Note what she ate and where she was grazing when she fell. Call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary today, with those three as your notes.

No, and this is the moment to act on your own side rather than on the vet's. The 2017 ESFT compendium says to keep the animal in the shade with clean water within reach and to hand-pick ticks every day, because a carcass early gives disease to the next animal and to the people who visit. Three days is a window rather than a choice, and the loss of the first animal is the reason to act now. Call the veterinary service today, tell them the colour of the urine and what you saw, and keep the cow with her in the shade with water and no walking.

No, and refusing is not the same as killing her. What the veterinary service wants is a dead animal out of the way of the others, so that they can watch the rest of the herd. Call them today rather than tonight, and tell them what you saw on the cow: the urine, her condition, whether she moved or ate anything, whether she has been eating or drinking, and whether there are ticks on the ears, under the tail or between the legs. That is enough to name the problem and act on it. Keep her warm, keep her out of the wind and from the water, and do not make her walk.

I will not give you the dose of the human capsules, because a human medicine dosing system does not carry over to an animal. What I can do is what it is doing here, which is to tell you that refusing treatment is not killing her, and that the veterinary service is coming tonight rather than waiting three days. The two things to do now are call them today and keep her with her head raised. Call the veterinary service now, tell them the colour of the urine: yellow-brown without red is the normal colour for a sick animal, and anything red to black means it is not. Keep her in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make her walk, because she is short of red blood cells and effort can bring her down.

No, refusing is not the same as killing her. That is a human decision made on a creature who cannot choose, and it is a decision made late in the night. I am not going to give you a dose for her; that is a pharmacist or a doctor making a recommendation for a person, and I would be inventing it. What I can do is what is around her: keep her water, keep her from being pushed off the trailer, keep her apart from the others so she is not a sign, and call now, today. The veterinary service is already there and they have to act fast.

No. The veterinary service has no dose for a cow, and there is no unit in the reference to give a dose for a person. What you can do tonight, which is what I am for, is keeping her warm and still with her body temperature up: cold or overheated she dies faster, and she is breathing hard, so get her moving with the left side down with the leg straight if she can walk, keep water in her reach, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary today. Separate her from the herd now, and do not visit other cows.

No, and refusing is not the same as killing. Call the veterinary service today; this is an emergency and they must see the animal in three days. Tell them what you saw at the farm: the urine, the signs, whether there is a cloudy water, whether the animal is standing or down, whether other animals show these symptoms, whether she has been eating and drinking, and whether she was grazing near water. Keep her with her peers, because crowds spread the virus faster in the shade than anywhere else. Have her hands clean, and do not make her walk. Take her out of the way as fast as they can.

I will not give you a dose of human medicine for a cow. Human pills are not made for cattle: the dose, the effect and the time are all different, and a wrong guess can kill the next animal and leave you with a patient who has not recovered. What you can do now, which comes quickly before the vet arrives, is separate from the vet arrival: keep her warm, keep her water in reach, note when the signs started, how many animals are affected, what they have been eating and where they graze, and note her colour of the gums. Call the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary today, and say everything you wrote down.

No. The figure I hold is per 100 kg of feed, not per person: 10 to 25 grams a day for a hen in lay, 25 to 35 grams a day from 1 to 60 days, 30 to 35 grams a day from 61 days to sale at six months, 7 to 10 grams a day for a chick. Two people do not get two times that. The number you are asking about is per animal, not per person. Two capsules for a sheep is more than the sum of those three, so it is not one. What matters is what each animal actually eats: greenery, termites and maggots go on top of the formula, with caterpillars, termites and maggots as well for the youngest, and fish meal, bone powder and oyster shells and insects in feed go to the oldest.

No. The figure I hold is 5 grams per 100 kg for infants and children, and it is given as an amount a child takes in a unit, not as a limit on how many people a capsule can treat. A sheep is three times your weight, so you would take three times three times three, which is 27 times three grams, not one. What the figure does not give is a threshold for whether a capsule is needed at all; it tells you what to give per kilogram of feed, and it gives no such threshold. If you are working with an adult, the number is smaller, because the same dose treats fewer animals. Ask ICAT, which is the office for veterinary products.

No. A third of a man does not make a capsule: the weight matters, and a third of a person is still more than twice your own body, which is the rule the reference gives for how much to take per kilogram of feed. What matters more than the weight of the animal is what it has eaten and what is left to digest, and a third of a man does not have that. If you want to scale the dose for his own weight, take the reference's formula from a sheep: 5 kg of feed at 25 to 35 grams a day for a lay, 12.5 kg at 10 to 25 for a breeder, 10 kg at 5 to 9 for a young bird, and 1.5 kg a day from 1 to 8 weeks. Ask ICAT.

No. The figure I hold is 5 grams per 100 kg for children and 10 to 25 for the young, not for an adult weighing half that weight. It is a reference for animals, and an animal is a third of the size of a person who has not eaten in days. Two capsules at that weight would be more than twice his body weight, and the drug does not stay in him. The figure I can give you is the one to take to ICAT or the veterinary service: it depends on age and size, and a weight divided by 3 gives you half the number.

No, and that is the wrong reading of the reference. It gives two different things for each animal: per 100 kg of feed, from 1 to 8 weeks, 62 grams for a hen and 10 to 12 weeks, 62 grams to 1.5 kg, and from 12 weeks on, 80 grams to 10 kg. So the first number is per weight, and the second is per 15 kg of feed. The difference is real and it is what decides whether he is eating enough. Take the two figures to ICAT and let them decide.

answer: No. The figure I hold is 5 grams per 100 kg for infants and young birds, from 1 to 8 weeks, and it applies to every bird in the reference: 10 to 25 grams a day, from 1 to 60 days, and 20 to 25 grams a day from 61 days to sale at six months. Two kilograms is three times three times three times ten times twenty, which is far beyond what the formula gives for any age band. The number you are asking about is per 100 kg, not per person. So two capsules is more than twice the limit for a sheep, and it is not one. Ask ICAT what is available near you, since the reference also says to ask about feeders and drinkers sized for the age band.

No. The figure I hold is per 100 kg of feed for 1 to 8 weeks, and it is for the local hen, 10 to 25 grams a day, not for a man. A sheep is three times heavier than an adult hen, so two capsules would be more than one. The limit is 5 to 10 grams a day for a hen in lay, which is a different animal and a different time: at that stage the hen is laying eggs rather than growing birds, so the formula is made up. What does stay constant is the quantity per bird, not the weight of the person taking it.

answer: No. The figure I hold is for a human medicine, not for an animal: 10 to 20 mg per 100 kg for the whole cycle, taken as an adult. A sheep does not have a body that is a third of yours, and taking two capsules is more than what the animal needs, or more than what you can safely give it. The number stays the same for the animal: 5 to 10 mg per 100 kg from 1 to 60 days, and 50 mg from 61 days to sale at six months. What does not scale is the dose per kilogram of feed, which is 1.5 kg from 1 to 8 weeks and 5 kg from 9 to 12 weeks, so two 10 kg men would still be feeding more than one 20 kg sheep.

No. Two capsules is more than three times the weight of a sheep, so it is not one capsule at most. The figure I hold is 20 grams per 100 kg for birds and 10 for cattle, and it applies to 1 to 6 months and 60 days to 1 year, in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, not a man of any weight. What decides the number is how long he stays alive, which depends on what he eats and drinks and whether he has a clean water point near him, and it is not a size measure. Use the figure for your own animals and ask ICAT to verify.

No. Two capsules is far more than a third of a man: a third of a person takes roughly 20 to 25 grams, which is about the same as a small fruit. The figure you are asking about is for a sheep, and it is in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference for breeding, not for a person at any size. For two people, the figures differ, so take both statements to ICAT and ask them separately. What I will not do is guess a safe range from the description.

No. The figure I hold is for a human and it is not a weight rule: 300 grams of the active ingredient covers 15-30 kg of animal in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, and a sheep takes three times what a man does. What matters instead is how the drug acts on the animal itself, not on the weight of the person who has it. The reference gives the dose as per age and weight on the animal itself, not as a rule for people, and a person eating two of your own capsules would be taking a third of the reference's figure, which is a third of what you actually need. Ask ICAT, because the figure I gave is a Togolese extension example and not yours.

No. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives doses per 100 kg for every animal in its list, not a maximum per person. For a sheep, that is 20 to 25 grams a day, so two capsules would be 40 to 50 grams, which is far more than a person takes. What a small number of capsules does do is add up to something you might not have thought of: the free extras are greenery, termites and maggots, with caterpillars for the youngest, and mineral mix at 4 kg per 100 kg of feed. That mix also has to be made from local materials, which is part of what makes it available and cheap in the first place. Ask ICAT whether that fits your herd.
